synthesis: Nothing passed as a full read today; six papers rated skim, none essential. If you want one, Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors (composing and steering diffusion models) or WASABI touch sampling theory relevant to Boltzmann generators. The landmark pick, RFdiffusion (2023), is worth revisiting as the diffusion-design reference point.

landmark.title: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion
landmark.abstract: Abstract There has been considerable recent progress in designing new proteins using deep-learning methods 1–9 . Despite this progress, a general deep-learning framework for protein design that enables solution of a wide range of design challenges, including de novo binder design and design of higher-order symmetric architectures, has yet to be described. Diffusion models 10,11 have had considerable success in image and language generative modelling but limited success when applied to protein modelling, probably due to the complexity of protein backbone geometry and sequence–structure relation
landmark.seed_title: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion
landmark.worth_30_min: RFdiffusion showed that fine-tuning a structure predictor (RoseTTAFold) as a denoiser over residue frames turns it into a general generative designer. It handles binders, symmetric oligomers and motif scaffolding, and designs were validated experimentally, including cryo-EM structures. It made diffusion over rigid-body frames the template for structure generation in AI for science, alongside AlphaFold-tier work.
landmark.inspiration: Molecules in a crystal are rigid or semi-rigid bodies with positions and orientations, which is the same SE(3) frame representation RFdiffusion denoises. That suggests diffusion-generated Z' packings, symmetry-conditioned generation in the spirit of space-group constraints, and motif or synthon scaffolding for conditional CSP. Diffusion-generated candidates could seed or replace GA initial pools such as Genarris, with DFT kept for final ranking.
landmark.foundations: Key ideas: denoising diffusion on Euclidean translations combined with diffusion on rotations (IGSO3), and pretrained-predictor-as-denoiser fine-tuning. Also self-conditioning, conditioning on partial structure (motifs), and symmetric noise for cyclic or dihedral assemblies. Finally, how to validate generated structures by in-silico refolding (AF2 self-consistency), which is analogous to re-relaxing generated crystals.
landmark.reading_guide: Read Fig. 1 and the opening sections on the method and the frame-diffusion setup (10 min). Then the symmetric oligomer and motif-scaffolding results (Figs. 2-3), which map best onto crystal symmetry (8 min). Then the Methods on rotation noise, self-conditioning and training loss (10 min). Skim the binder design experiments and wet-lab assay details.

items.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
items.abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Acros

items.title: Trajectory Matching: Discrete Flow Matching with Structured Actions
items.abstract: The natural units of structured discrete generation are often not independent single-component edits but richer actions: attaching a fragment to a molecule, inserting a node together with an incident edge, or growing a hierarchy by adding a child. Yet most existing discrete flow matching methods (DFM) are restricted to independent component-wise edits over fixed-size states. This restriction stems from endpoint conditioning: endpoints fix the source and target during training but not the action sequence between them, making tractable conditional rates hard to define for complex actions that cannot be factorized component-wise. We propose trajectory matching, which conditions the flow on a full sequence of actions connecting the endpoints. This yields principled, simulation-free training targets for user-defined action spaces, including actions that change state size, modify multiple components, or depend on earlier actions. We prove that the resulting objective recovers the marginal flow and that trajectory matching strictly subsumes factorized DFM, while additionally capturing actions with prerequisite structure such as hierarchy growth or fragment-based molecule generation. items.title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
items.abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly

items.title: WASABI: Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants
items.abstract: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.

items.title: EVA-Flow: Learning Shared Chemistry for Unified Environment-Aware Molecular Conformation Generation
items.abstract: Molecular 3D structures underpin simulations of thermodynamics, kinetics, crystallization, and nucleation, making their accurate prediction central to drug discovery and materials design. However, molecular geometry can change dramatically across environments. Existing models either ignore environmental effects or train separate models for each environment. We hypothesize that transfer learning across contexts is possible for conformer generation and that a general model will perform better when training data are limited, as in ligand binding and crystallization. We introduce EVA-Flow, a unified framework for environment-aware molecular conformation generation that learns shared chemical structure and adapts it through environment-conditioned generative modeling. Across vacuum, protein-ligand docking, solvation, and crystal packing, pretraining and cross-environment finetuning provide their largest gains in the three data-scarce settings. Evaluation against multiple reference conformations shows that EVA-Flow covers a broad range of solvation conformations. Analyses of molecules shared across environments support its ability to generate different conformations for the same molecule

items.title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
items.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery
